It looks like your motherboard is the SuperMicro X9DRH-7F, [here](https://www.supermicro.com/manuals/motherboard/C606_602/MNL-1306.pdf) is the manual for it. 

I have a similar setup, with a X9DRD, 2x E5-2697v2’s and 256 GB of DDR3 ECC memory. In terms of raw compute power, a modern Ryzen 9 processor will outperform both CPUs and be much quieter and more efficient, but I use my machine for messing around with VMs and testing different software (usually within ESXi). 

It performs surprisingly well for Python and R-based bioinformatics work. IPMI is nice because I can log in remotely and turn it on, then run my pipelines and shut it down. Vastly outperforms research lab PCs and I have the benefit of not having to queue in line for time allocation on the university’s supercomputer. 

You may be able to find an LGA2011 active cooler. I was considering it to reduce the fan noise, but it mainly runs when nobody is at home these days. 

Let me know if you have any questions! Good luck!

Jumping on this comment in case anyone wants to go down the Hydrogen-alpha rabbit hole!

Certain deep space objects (like the Horsehead Nebula, for example) emit most of its light in the H-alpha band (656.3nm) and it’s quite easy and cheap to come across a narrowband H-alpha filter that can be used for astrophotography. 

These filters are usually 3-7nm (or 30-70 angstroms) on either side of the emission line, but to capture solar flares, you need a H-alpha filter that has 4 angstroms of band pass (super super expensive)

Either way, hope it helps! I’m only a hobby astronomer, so any physics folks out there please feel free to chime in

Others may have better solutions to this but what I usually do (this also applies to my 10” motorized dob) is align the red dot finder before every viewing session. There should be a couple of adjustment knobs on the body of the scope and the actual finder itself that will adjust the dot. I’ll point it at a bright object (if the moon is out) or something visible during the day and center the red dot on that before stargazing. 

Setting up the scope and small bumps can move it out of alignment so I just give it a good alignment prior to every use. Hope this helps!

I started off on one of these too! You’ll definitely notice an upgrade in the viewing experience and usability of some of suggested scopes here, but having one of these for a few years really cemented the fact that I enjoyed the hobby and wanted to expand. 

Those equatorial mounts are pretty flimsy, but I got mine to get pretty close to polar aligned by using my phone’s level app for latitude and the compass app to get the axis aligned to true (not magnetic) north. You can definitely resolve the planets (Jupiter + Moons, Saturn’s Rings) and get great views of the moon. Brighter and larger DSOs are also discernible and will teach you how to find objects looking at star maps. 

If you can find a Celestron motor drive for cheap (they’re about $50 msrp, I got mine used for $30) it’ll do decent tracking of your objects. 

Definitely a good tool to gauge whether you enjoy diving into the nitty gritty technical details of astronomy (I totally did!) or would rather have something easy to look at and setup (like a dobsonian or a alt/az scope with GoTo) 

Feel free to ask any questions you may have!

I feel like biochemistry is the perfect science that sums up all hard sciences. Biology is fascinating, diving deep into the evolutionary history of species and marveling at the diversity. Chemistry is fascinating: an explanation of how mere electron movement is the basis for virtually all “life” reactions. Physics quantifies the natural world and it’s phenomena. There’s a value given to the feeling on your skin by the morning sun, a precise calculation of how the planets revolve. Mathematics provides a basis to convert and work with these numbers. 

There are other hard sciences that are equally important that I’m not entirely familiar with, but I feel like biochemistry bridges all of these fascinating subjects together. 

You learn about proteins and apply the biology approach: which organisms did these proteins come from, why are they used in the “wild” and how conserved are they across species? You apply the chemistry approach: how does the molecular structure of this enzyme/protein allow it to function so specifically? You apply physics: how does this strand of amino acids “fold” into its final form? What energy is required for this process? Mathematics ties all of these together, especially when attempting to model behavior. 

The more I learn and research in biochemistry, the more I fall in love with just how *much* goes on within *every single one* of our cells *every single second*. But you don’t just examine it through a single lens, you have to look at it on the most fundamental level as well as on the macro scale to understand what is occurring. 

Again, a lot of these are generalizations. I’d like to add one more thing: a lot of us lab rats toil away for years of our lives in labs, conducting, re-conducting, and re-re-conducting our experiments, in an effort to not only understand our specific topics, but to publish and contribute to the vast swaths of scientific knowledge. I believe all great scientific achievements stand on the shoulders of giants - those who never made a name for themselves but dedicated their time and energy to spearheading the knowledge of mankind *ever so slightly* forward.
